Dear Contest Curator,

Thank you for inviting us to probe the power and limits of language through correspondence.  
The piece I submitted, “A Letter to George,” is built on a single, sustained epistolary voice: a widow addressing her deceased husband, George, from the cramped desk of a retail case‑manager. By choosing the letter form, the story forces the narrator to, word by word, negotiate what can be spoken about loss, love, and the everyday absurdities that persist after death.  

The creative idea is to juxtapose the grand, timeless ritual of a mourning missive with a stream of mundane, almost comic details—wrong lunches, ant containers, impatient customers, a new cat named Misty, and the clumsy humor of a friend’s fictional police car anecdote. Each anecdote is a linguistic foothold that the narrator uses to keep George present, yet each also reveals the insufficiency of words to fully capture the ache of absence.  

Interwoven are flash‑memories of church, friends, and a new romance with a hospice chaplain. The letter becomes a catalogue of “what‑ifs” (if George had bought a newer car, if he had spoken more for himself) and a litany of gratitude, showing how language can both memorialize and reshape reality. By ending with a poem written by the new partner, the story underlines how different voices can attempt to fill the same void, while acknowledging that none can replace the original.  

Thus, the piece explores how a letter can be both a bridge and a barrier: it lets the living speak to the dead, but also exposes the moments when language simply falls short, echoing Shakespeare’s “words, words, words.”  

Yours in letters,  
[Your Name]
